newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac to speak out on French "cohabitation".
newsitem.headline: Chirac to speak out on French "cohabitation".

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac gives his first television interview on Monday since his centre-right coalition lost a parliamentary election on June 1, amputating him of most of his power.

Chirac is expected to comment on his uneasy "cohabitation" with Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's left-wing government, highlighted by its decision to halt the privatisation of defence electronics group Thomson-CSF, which he launched.

The president who reviews the annual Bastille Day military parade on Monday before giving an hour-long television interview at 1100 GMT is a mere shadow of the brash, self-confident leader who took office two years ago and began by resuming nuclear tests.

Diplomats expect Chirac may try to nudge the government towards making a fresh effort to cut the budget deficit to ensure France qualfies for a single European currency, but he is unlikely to seek a confrontation with Jospin.

The government announced on Friday it would keep a decisive stake in Thomson, which makes missiles, radars, command systems and avionics, and would seek to build a French defence electronics pole around it while seeking European alliances.

Chirac may comment on the strategic implictions of the move, denounced by his conservative Gaullist supporters as a "historic error" that could shut France out of the restructuring of Europe's arms industry.
But an aide said the president's main thrust would be to "take a far-sighted, elevated view of France's future, tracing long-term perspectives" and not pick fights with Jospin.

Analysts say he is too weak to challenge the government for the moment, having effectively lost control of the Gaullist party he founded to left-leaning nationalist Philippe Seguin, and he will have to restore his own popularity and see Jospin's fall before he can do so.

Chirac has looked gloomy, fidgeting nervously at public events, since he devastated his own presidency by dissolving parliament and calling an early poll 10 months ahead of schedule in a gamble that backfired.

"Since the election, he looks as if he has had the stuffing knocked out of him, but it would be foolish to write him off. He knows cohabitation well and he's a specialist at comebacks," a senior European diplomat said.
Chirac served as prime minister in 1986-88 under Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, who outfoxed him and easily won re-election in 1988.
On the international stage, where the president has most of his remaining power under the constitution, France's hybrid executive has worked relatively harmoniously so far.
The price has been relative isolation both in NATO, where Paris is traditionally the odd-man-out, and, more worryingly, in the European Union.

Chirac and Jospin agreed that conditions were not ripe for France to rejoin NATO's military command after the United States rejected Paris's demand that it hand over the key southern command, which controls the Mediterranean, to a European.
France has not found support among EU partners, notably from key ally Germany, for its call for Brussels to fund job-creating public works projects to help revive growth.

Franco-German relations are in an unusually prickly state, partly because of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's domestic woes, but also due to the Jospin government's refusal to impose more austerity to meet a strict reading of the terms for the euro.
On economic and monetary union, Chirac may recall that his Socialist predecessor signed the Maastricht treaty and gave France's word that it will meet the criteria.

But it would be hard for him to blame the new government, since a handover note by former Gaullist prime minister Alain Juppe leaked last week acknowledged that the 1997 budget deficit was well above the three percent of gross domestic product target set by the treaty, and heading for 4.0 percent next year.
